name: Spatial Proportions and Cognitive Processing Mode — How Ceiling Height and Room Geometry Modulate Abstract vs. Concrete Cognition
short_description: High ceilings promote abstract, relational, creative cognition; low ceilings promote concrete, detail-oriented cognition; transitions between heights amplify the effect through PE
structural_pattern: Spatial proportions — particularly ceiling height, but also room width-to-depth ratio and degree of enclosure — modulate cognitive processing style. High ceilings (>3m) and spatially expansive proportions promote abstract, relational, creative cognition. Low ceilings (<2.5m) and spatially constrained proportions promote concrete, detail-oriented, item-specific cognition. The multi-level mechanism: LEVEL 1 (Neural): Low ceilings activate the amygdala (Vartanian et al., 2013), producing a mild threat/confinement signal. LEVEL 2 (Affective): The threat/safety signal modulates affect via Fredrickson's broaden-and-build — safety → positive affect → cognitive broadening. LEVEL 3 (Conceptual): The cognitive broadening/narrowing is semantically labeled as 'freedom' (high ceiling) or 'confinement' (low ceiling). PE ADDITION: The processing-style effect should be largest at TRANSITIONS between spatial proportions because the PE is greatest when the spatial prediction changes.
higher_order_principle: Architecture as cognitive modulator. Spatial proportions do not merely produce aesthetic responses (T2 Goldilocks) or navigational responses (SC1) — they modulate the brain's processing mode, affecting creativity, attention to detail, and abstract reasoning. This connects architecture to cognitive performance outcomes (A9 Task Environment) through a spatial mechanism: the room you are in shapes how you think, not just how you feel.
transition_pe_hypothesis: Processing-style effect should be LARGEST at transitions between ceiling heights (moving from low to high) because PE is greatest at the moment of spatial prediction violation. Moving from a 2.4m corridor to a 6m atrium should produce a larger cognitive-broadening effect than being in the 6m atrium from the start. UNTESTED — critical experiment.

causal_links.evidence_base: High ceilings → reduced enclosure → lower amygdala activation. Low ceilings → increased enclosure → elevated amygdala activation. Vartanian et al. (2013) fMRI evidence. Connects to SC2 (isovist vertical dimension) and T5 (threat).

Positive affect (from spatial openness) → broadened cognition → abstract, relational, creative processing. Neutral/negative affect (from spatial constriction) → narrowed cognition → concrete, detail-oriented processing. Fredrickson (2001, ~3,000 citations). Meyers-Levy & Zhu (2007): ceiling height mediates through freedom/confinement concepts.

PE-specific prediction: the processing-style effect should be LARGEST at transitions between ceiling heights, not in static conditions, because the PE is greatest at the moment of spatial prediction violation. UNTESTED — critical experiment.

scope_conditions: Applies to occupied buildings where cognitive tasks are performed — offices, schools, libraries, hospitals, studios
Effect is strongest for tasks with variable processing requirements; purely physical tasks may not be affected
The magnitude of the ceiling height effect in the original study (10 ft vs. 8 ft = 0.6m difference) is substantial; smaller differences may not produce detectable effects
Interacts with spatial function: a deliberately low-ceilinged reading nook may be experienced as cozy (positive) rather than confining (negative) because the low ceiling matches the function
moderators: Task type: creative tasks benefit most from high ceilings; detail-oriented tasks may benefit from low ceilings
Cultural expectations: ceiling-height norms differ across cultures and building types
Other spatial features: window size, lighting, color, and material warmth all modulate the affective response to ceiling height
Duration: extended time in a space may lead to adaptation, attenuating the processing-style effect

interactions.nature: Ceiling height determines the vertical dimension of the isovist/prediction volume. VF3 extends SC2's horizontal-emphasis to the vertical processing-style effect.
Low ceilings may activate T5 confinement-threat pathway. VF3 extends T5's threat response to cognitive processing-style modulation.

Ceiling height transitions are a primary component of the compression-release technique in SC3. VF3 adds the cognitive-processing dimension: compression (low ceiling) → concrete processing; release (high ceiling) → abstract processing.
Reverse link added by CX V12 S3 remediation to satisfy bidirectional interaction encoding.
